_doc: McCready's Opera House (#1143): the building lab's step 2 as a DESIGN, written by tools/buildings/opera_house_spec.py (edit it, not this). NOT BUILT: the build waits for after the slice and Sean's OK on the sheet and plan; the builder's new parts are listed in experiments/building_lab/opera_house/README.md. Sizes here, the look on the sheet (experiments/building_lab/opera_house/sheet).

identity.owner: Ezra McCready, who sold his share in the Argentine lode in 1880 and built the town something to be proud of (and a stage for his wife's sister)
identity.trade: an opera house: travelling companies, melodrama, a singer with the band, lectures, the magic lantern, the Fourth of July ball, the Miners' Union meetings
identity.means: the only brick building in Salt Creek but the bank: freighted-in brick, plate glass, iron, 480 opera chairs from Chicago, scenery painted in Denver
identity.age_and_repair: 1 year: the brick new and sharp, the walk already worn at the doors; one window in the lane boarded where a drunk put a bottle through
clues: a stack of old show bills behind the box office
cigar ash ground into the foyer's carpet
a banjo case and a pair of dancing shoes left in a dressing room
chalk seat numbers on the backs of the chairs
a bucket of sand and a bucket of water by every footlight

lot._doc: PROPOSED new lot (Sean, 2026-11-24): valley.json town.north past the undertaker's (x 106-128): a lane x 128.0-130.4 (8 ft, the hall's side exit), the lot x 130.4-149.0, 18.6 m (61 ft) by the town's 125 ft depth to Back Street. Main Street's and Back Street's x [-125, 130] grow to 150 (the East Road still leaves from x 130 to the south-east; at x 149 its north edge is at z ~+2, clear of the walk). The ground (probed 2026-11-24, ValleyTerrain.height): -0.44 (west) to -0.58 (east) at the front line, +0.18..+0.06 at 20 m back, +0.84..+0.38 at 30 m (Back Street's bank): 0.65-1.0 m of rise to the back wall, so a pad dug level at the walk's street edge (saloon B's) with a bank left behind the yard.

walk.why: A brick front needs no awning; three wide stone-edged steps at the doors for a crowd and ladies' skirts.

levels._doc: The hall's floor at the walk's top; the stage 3 ft 6 in over it; the foyer and the balcony's back 5 m over it (the lobby's ceiling 15 ft); the hall 32 ft to its plaster ceiling under the trusses' bottom chords; the stage house 13.5 m (roll drops: a small town's stage didn't fly its scenery).

frame._doc: NEW: a load-bearing brick building with timber floors and roof. Walls from Kidder's Building Construction and Superintendence (public halls: 17 in to 40 ft), lime mortar; the hall's roof on Howe trusses (timber chords and diagonals, iron rods for the verticals: Haupt, Hatfield) spanning the 57 ft between the side walls at 12 ft centres, bearing on brick pilasters; the balcony and upper floors on joists in pockets in the brick.

brick_wall._doc: NEW (`BrickWall`): bricks in courses (8 x 4 x 2.25 in, 3/8 in joints), common bond (a header course every sixth), each member a run of bricks a course high, so a ball chips a face and a charge brings down courses (masonry lab: brick as its kind); dressed stone quoins, base, sills and keystones as the jail's stone pieces

joist._doc: 3 x 12 at 16 in: the balcony and the foyer at 100 lb/ft2 (a crowd standing), the dance floor's 70 too

walls._doc: The front on Main Street (facing south): red brick, stone quoins at both corners, a stone base course to the walk, stone sills and keystones; three arched doorways in the middle (a pair of cast-iron columns either side of the middle one), an arched window either side; five tall arched foyer windows over them, five small arched windows in the attic storey; the galvanized-iron cornice on brackets, its frieze MCCREADY'S OPERA HOUSE in gilt, the pediment's roundel 1881.

openings._doc: a pair of panelled and glazed doors 5 ft 6 in by 10 ft, a fanlight in the arch; outward for a crowd leaving (Chicago's code after 1871's fire)

walls._doc: The east side, on the open ground where the East Road leaves town: plainer brick, pilasters between four tall arched windows (iron fire shutters), the stage house rising at the back.

openings._doc: the hall's side exit to the lane, by the boxes
the hall's back exit, from the cross aisle under the balcony
the scenery door, at the stage's height: flats and trunks off a wagon's bed

walls._doc: The west side, on the 8 ft lane to the undertaker's: as the east, its windows the same (they look at his wall, 3 m off); the lane is the hall's second way out.

openings._doc: the hall's side exit to the lane, by the boxes
the hall's back exit, from the cross aisle under the balcony

walls._doc: The back, on the yard and Back Street: the stage door up four steps, the scenery door at the stage's height (a wagon backs up to it: the yard's ground and a wagon bed are near the stage's level), the dressing rooms' windows on two floors.

openings._doc: the stage door, to the dressing rooms' corridor

walls._doc: The vestibule's back: the box office's wall (east) and the cloak room's (west), plaster on brick.

openings._doc: into the lobby: three pairs under one arch, held open
the ticket window, onto the vestibule: a brass grille and a marble shelf

walls._doc: The lobby's back wall (12 in brick, the balcony's back rests on it): the doors into the hall's cross aisle under the balcony.

The proscenium wall: 13 in brick from the footing to the roof (the stage's fire wall), the arch 28 ft wide and 20 ft high over the stage, framed in gilt plaster; doors either side from the boxes' passages to the wings.

openings._doc: the proscenium opening over the stage's floor
the stage's back door to the corridor

balcony._doc: NEW (a curved balcony, `Balcony.horseshoe`): the deck's rows stepped up toward the walls (0.3 m a row), its rail's line a horseshoe; the curve laid as straight segments of 0.6 m (each a joist bay: a ball or a charge brings down a segment, not the whole sweep). The front a panelled, gilded fascia on the rail's line; cast-iron columns (6 in, hollow: they shatter, they don't bend) under it.

boxes.front: curved, velvet rail, gilt; drapes tied back

seats._doc: Folding theatre chairs on cast-iron standards screwed to the floor in rows (the front four rows on runners, cleared for a ball: Sean's dances). The floor is level: a dance floor too.

stage._doc: NEW (`Stage`): saloon B's stage grown up: a raised floor of members on joists and posts, an apron with the footlights' trough, a trap between two joists (the church's hatch rule), the drop curtain and three roll drops on battens hung from the gridiron, wings of flats, a pin rail with ropes (the Rope part). Lit by the footlights and border lamps (OilLamps).
drops: drop curtain: a painted lake under mountains in a painted gilt frame

cornice._doc: NEW (`Cornice`, shared with the hotel): galvanized sheet iron on a timber frame, painted stone-colour, its brackets in pairs, a frieze for the gilt name (the game's own lettering)

posters: THE MORTGAGE ON HAZEL FARM, or a Daughter's Sacrifice: a melodrama in four acts
The Hartwell Shakespearean Company: HAMLET and RICHARD III, two nights only
Professor Alcott's Magic Lantern: Wonders of the Yellowstone, sixty views
Signor Valetti, Prestidigitator: the Vanishing Lady
Miss Lottie Byrne, the Colorado Nightingale, with the Salt Creek Cornet Band

rooms.use: a show night's crowd in out of the street; tickets bought at the window, bills on the walls
the ticket seller behind the grille, the cash box, the seating chart, the night's takings
the two stairs up to the foyer and balcony, the inner doors to the hall; waiting, smoking, the interval
the parquet: ~312 seats; the crowd's place; a ball with the front rows cleared
the band: a piano, a fiddle, a cornet; a rail before the first row
the acts (#1143's later shows); the wings either side of the arch, the pin rail on the west wall, roll drops and flats; a trap in the middle
the footlights along its edge (kerosene, tin reflectors), the curtain's line behind it
the stage door to the stage; the stair to the upper dressing rooms
the balcony's foyer: the five tall windows over Main Street, settees, the interval's promenade
McCready's office over the box office: the safe, the bookings, the window on the street
the horseshoe: ~152 seats, the cheaper ones at the back
four more dressing rooms off the corridor's stair, the wardrobe

stairs._doc: the lobby's east stair, outer flight: up toward the back to the landing (1 m deep, both flights' width) against the lobby's back wall; a turned walnut newel, a red runner on brass rods (the hotel's stair as a part)
the inner flight, back toward the front, arriving at the foyer

the lobby's west stair, outer flight: up toward the back to the landing (1 m deep, both flights' width) against the lobby's back wall; a turned walnut newel, a red runner on brass rods (the hotel's stair as a part)
the inner flight, back toward the front, arriving at the foyer
a steep boxed stair in the corridor (a ladder-stair: its going to the spec at build)

materials._doc: From the material library by name when built; new: brick, sandstone, plaster on lath, wallpaper, red plush, gilt, galvanized iron. Floors `floor_fir_worn`; the lobby's woods walnut (FN3 is parked: its walnut figure needs the material lab first).

sources: F. E. Kidder, Building Construction and Superintendence (1890s eds.): brick wall thicknesses for public halls
Herman Haupt, General Theory of Bridge Construction (1851) and Hatfield, The American House-Carpenter (1880): Howe trusses
Central City Opera House (1878, stone, ~550 seats) and the Tabor Opera House, Leadville (1879, brick, three storeys): size and arrangement
Wright Opera House, Ouray (1888): a cast-iron front on a mining-town opera house (a little late: the columns only)
A. H. Andrews & Co. (Chicago) opera-chair catalogues, 1880s: 20 in seats on cast-iron standards, 30-32 in rows
